study_identification.title: Lifespan development of thalamic nuclei and characterizing thalamic nuclei abnormalities in schizophrenia using normative modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: This study aimed to characterize age effects on thalamic nuclei volumes across the lifespan using normative models, clarify the association between cognition and thalamic nuclei volumes over time, and determine the frequency of thalamic structural abnormalities in individuals with schizophrenia using normative deviation scores.

dataset_name.answer: HCP Development; HCP S1200; HCP Aging

hc_n.answer: 1952 (HCP S1200 n=825, HCP Development n=525, HCP Aging n=602)

hc_age.answer: Overall: mean 34.5, sd 19.9, min 5.60, max 100; Development: mean 14.8, sd 3.97, min 5.60, max 21.9; Young Adult: mean 28.7, sd 3.76, min 22.0, max 37.0; Aging: mean 59.6, sd 15.4, min 36.0, max 100

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: HCP PreFreeSurfer pipeline for HCP Lifespan Cohort (bias field corrected structural T1 images in native subject space); THOMAS (Thalamus Optimized Multi-Atlas Segmentation) for thalamic nuclei segmentation

quality_checking_detail.answer: Visual inspection for visible artifacts including motion artifacts before thalamic segmentation. THOMAS segmentations were visually inspected by overlaying representative slices on T1 images. Individuals excluded if segmentation included voxels outside the thalamus or missed voxels within the thalamus. Exclusion rates varied by sample: Development (1.08% poor T1 quality, 14.72% poor thalamus segmentation, 3.53% failed segmentation), Young Adult S1200 (0% poor T1 quality, 2.88% poor thalamus segmentation, 0.18% failed segmentation), Aging (4.69% poor T1 quality, 7.86% poor thalamus segmentation, 4.41% failed segmentation).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: ComBat harmonization using neuroCombat R package to adjust for site and scanner effects. Raw thalamic nuclei volumes were harmonized for 12 sites (HCP Lifespan Cohort included 9 sites; Schizophrenia Cohort included 3 sites), with age, sex, race, and diagnoses included as covariates to preserve during harmonization. ComBat models batch effects as additive and multiplicative components using an empirical Bayesian framework.

response_variable.answer: Thalamic nuclei volumes (9 nuclei per hemisphere: anteroventral (AV), ventral anterior (VA), ventrolateral (VL), ventral posterolateral (VPL), pulvinar (PU), lateral geniculate (LGN), medial geniculate (MGN), centromedian (CM), mediodorsal (MD))

predictor_variables.answer: Age; Sex; Race; Estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV)

predictor_effects.answer: Age modeled with natural cubic splines (2 equally-spaced knots over age range 5-100 years) for nonlinear effects on mean (μ), variance (σ), and shape (ν) parameters of generalized gamma distribution. Sex, race, and eTIV modeled as fixed effects. Family membership included as random intercepts to account for correlation between participants from same families. Natural logarithm linkage function for μ and σ, identity linkage function for ν.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses multiple sources of nuisance structure. Site and scanner effects were handled through ComBat harmonization modeling additive and multiplicative batch effects. Age nonlinearity was addressed through natural cubic splines in GAMLSS framework. The model accounts for heteroscedasticity by modeling variance (σ) as a function of age and other covariates. Family structure (clustering) was handled through random intercepts for family membership. Race and intracranial volume were included as covariates. The GAMLSS framework models location, scale, and shape parameters, addressing distributional assumptions comprehensively.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To account for site effects, we used ComBat to adjust for site and scanner effects on both the HCP Lifespan Cohort and our Schizophrenia Cohort using the neuroCombat R package... ComBat models the batch effects as additive and multiplicative components in the data and uses an empirical Bayesian framework... Normative modeling of thalamic nuclei change over the lifespan was conducted using generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS); a robust and flexible framework for modeling nonlinear growth trajectories. GAMLSS models were fitted to thalamic nuclei volumes separately for each hemisphere to model nonlinear age effects (on the outcome mean and variance) over the lifespan (ranging 5-100), stratified by sex, race, intracranial volumes and included random intercepts for families to account for the correlation between participants from the same families in the HCP Lifespan Cohort.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: While the paper reports model fitting details and spline estimates (Supplementary Table 6), there is no explicit mention of within-sample validation metrics such as explained variance, MSLL, cross-validation, or residual diagnostics on the training data (HCP Lifespan cohort). The focus appears to be on model specification and fitting rather than formal validation within the same domain.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Spline estimates for each model are presented in the Supplemental Materials. Supplementary Table 6 shows spline estimates for mu and sigma from GAMLSS models for all thalamic nuclei.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study validated the normative model on an independent healthy control group (N=211) from the Schizophrenia Cohort. The validation tested whether individuals from this independent sample fell within the expected normative range (5th-95th centile). Results showed that a median of 85.3% of healthy individuals fell within the 90% normative range across all thalamic subdivisions, demonstrating reasonable generalization to an independent sample from the same domain (healthy individuals).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: The validity of this model was tested using our healthy control group, and we identified the proportion of individuals who fell within 90% of the population. Across all thalamic subdivisions, a median of 85.3% of healthy individuals fell within the 90% range, indicating that the normative models generalized reasonably well to an independent sample.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study applied the normative models trained on healthy individuals (HCP Lifespan cohort) to a different domain—individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (N=234). This represents cross-domain validation where the model is tested on a clinically distinct population. The models successfully identified elevated proportions of individuals with infra-normal volumes in the schizophrenia group compared to healthy controls, demonstrating clinical utility and generalization across domains.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Application of the normative references generated from healthy HCP samples to an independent group of healthy individuals and patients with schizophrenia revealed a significantly higher proportion of patients with infra-normal bilateral mediodorsal, pulvinar, and medial geniculate nuclei volumes. Other nuclei also showed higher frequencies of individuals with infra-normal volumes, ranging between 9-18% across nuclei.

clinical_dataset.answer: Schizophrenia cohort (repository study comprising data from three neuroimaging projects: CT00762866, R01MH070560, R01MH102266)

clinical_groups_age.answer: SCZ: mean 29.2, sd 11.0, median 24.9, min 15.6, max 60.5

deviation_metric.answer: Centile scores (individual quantile positions relative to age-, sex-, race-, and eTIV-adjusted normative distributions from GAMLSS models). Individuals categorized as infra-normal (below 5th centile), normal (5th-95th centile), or supra-normal (above 95th centile).

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group differences in centile scores between healthy controls and schizophrenia groups were tested using Wilcoxon rank sum test for independent samples. Differences in proportions of individuals with infra- and supra-normal volumes were tested using Pearson's Chi-squared test. Associations between deviation (centile) scores and cognitive function (SCIP composite z-score) were tested using Spearman's rho. For comparison, associations between age/sex/race/ICV-standardized raw volumes and cognition were also examined. FDR correction was applied for multiple comparisons across 18 nuclei (9 per hemisphere).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Up to 18% of individuals with schizophrenia exhibited abnormally small mediodorsal and pulvinar volumes (below 5th centile), and centile deviation scores showed stronger associations with cognitive impairment than raw volumes.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Group comparisons revealed significantly lower median centiles in schizophrenia vs. controls for bilateral pulvinar (Right: SZ=0.287 vs HC=0.477, p<0.001; Left: SZ=0.321 vs HC=0.478, p<0.001), mediodorsal (Right: SZ=0.311 vs HC=0.513, p<0.001; Left: SZ=0.346 vs HC=0.496, p<0.001), centromedian, medial geniculate, and other nuclei. Chi-square tests showed significantly increased proportions of infra-normal volumes in schizophrenia for bilateral pulvinar (17.5% right, 15.0% left) and mediodorsal (14.1% right, 17.9% left) compared to controls (~5%). No increased frequency of supra-normal volumes was observed. Centile scores showed significant associations with cognition (SCIP) in schizophrenia for bilateral mediodorsal (Right rho=0.241, p=0.004; Left rho=0.206, p=0.016) and pulvinar (Right rho=0.185, p=0.022; Left rho=0.198, p=0.016), while standardized raw volumes showed no significant associations. In the normative HCP sample, associations between executive function and mediodorsal/pulvinar volumes shifted from negative in development (reflecting maturation-related volume decreases) to positive in adults (larger volumes associated with better function).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The dataset for normative modeling was cross-sectional rather than longitudinal; age effects may differ between cross-sectional and longitudinal data. Modeling started at age 5, missing early developmental period especially critical for sensory nuclei like lateral geniculate. Data harmonization was necessary due to multiple scanning parameters across projects, limiting direct applicability to novel datasets without adaptation. Alternative factors co-segregating with schizophrenia (antipsychotic medication, adverse lifestyle factors like substance use) may contribute to observed deviations. Whether deviation patterns are specific to schizophrenia or transcend diagnostic categories is unknown.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Deviation scores may serve as a better metric than raw volumes for examining brain-behavior associations in clinical samples, as they account for variation observed in the general population. This approach is particularly valuable for smaller patient samples. The study demonstrates that while case-control differences are robust, only a minority of patients demonstrate unusually small thalamic nuclei volumes. Normative modeling enables identification of these individuals, which is a necessary step toward precision medicine in psychiatry.

general_notes.general_notes: The study used THOMAS (Thalamus Optimized Multi-Atlas Segmentation) for thalamic nuclei segmentation, which has greater reliability than FreeSurfer and performed well compared to manual segmentation. The multi-atlas was created from 20 white-matter nulled MPRAGE datasets acquired at 7T resolution. Of the 12 THOMAS subdivisions, habenula and mammillothalamic tract were excluded, and anterior/posterior ventrolateral nuclei were combined into single ventrolateral nucleus, resulting in 9 nuclei analyzed per hemisphere. The study found heterogeneous developmental trajectories: association nuclei (mediodorsal, centromedian) showed steep volume reductions through childhood/adolescence stabilizing in adulthood then declining in aging; sensorimotor nuclei (lateral geniculate, ventral posterolateral) remained stable through youth/adulthood then declined in aging. Neuropsychological assessment differed between cohorts: HCP used NIH Toolbox executive function composite (Flanker, Dimensional Card Sort, Pattern Completion), while Schizophrenia Cohort used SCIP composite z-score. The Schizophrenia Cohort was collected at single location with three scanning parameter sets. Full site information for data harmonization is provided in Supplementary Table 4.
